summary_paragraph: A man with a history of CAD, CABG, COPD, CVA, and long-term alcohol abuse was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. Initial workup revealed elevated liver enzymes, fatty liver, and gallstones, but imaging ruled out cholecystitis. A diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis was made, supported by clinical history and lab findings. An endoscopy showed mild esophagitis and diffuse gastritis. He was managed supportively with thiamine, folic acid, multivitamins, and acid suppression. His platelet count, which was initially low, improved during the admission, allowing restart of Plavix. Urinary incontinence was attributed to detrusor instability, and oxybutynin was restarted. Liver function tests improved steadily. He was discharged home with home health services, new medications including rifaximin, and follow-up plans with primary care, hepatology, and GI. Alcohol cessation was strongly emphasized.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, continuous
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
